solution: Change the division to multiplication by the reciprocal, that is, flip the second fraction: $\frac{{=k}x+{=k*a}}{x^2-{=b*b}}\times\frac{x+{=b}}{x+{=a}}$

Factorise: take out the common factor, ${=k}x+{=k*a}={=k}(x+{=a})$, and use the difference of two squares, $x^2-{=b*b}=(x-{=b})(x+{=b})$: $=\frac{{=k}(x+{=a})}{(x-{=b})(x+{=b})}\times\frac{x+{=b}}{x+{=a}}$
Cancel the common factors $(x+{=a})$ and $(x+{=b})$: $=\frac{{=k}}{x-{=b}}$
families.notes: Entry point of the skill: the book's we19 method (flip the second fraction, factorise, cancel) with only two kinds of factorising, a common factor and a difference of two squares, and no trinomial. Instance = k(x+a)/(x^2-b^2) divided by (x+a)/(x+b); answer is always k/(x-b), a single reduced fraction, so the marker uses form 'simplest'. Constraint a != b keeps the two cancelled factors distinct (a == b would still be correct but muddles which factor cancels). b >= 2 so x^2 - b^2 never prints as x^2 - 1. Verified by exact rational evaluation at several x over all 320 parameter combinations. The stem keeps the book's 'assume all denominators are non-zero' wording (strictly the divisor is also non-zero, x != -a, which the book leaves implicit). 320 distinct instances.

solution: Change the division to multiplication by the reciprocal, that is, flip the second fraction: $\frac{x^2+{=p+q}x+{=p*q}}{{=c}(x^2-{=q*q})}\times\frac{{=n}x^2-{=n*q}x}{{=d}x^2+{=d*p}x}$
Factorise every numerator and denominator: $x^2+{=p+q}x+{=p*q}=(x+{=p})(x+{=q})$, $x^2-{=q*q}=(x-{=q})(x+{=q})$, ${=d}x^2+{=d*p}x={=d}x(x+{=p})$ and ${=n}x^2-{=n*q}x={=n}x(x-{=q})$
Write the product with every factor showing: $\frac{(x+{=p})(x+{=q})}{{=c}(x-{=q})(x+{=q})}\times\frac{{=n}x(x-{=q})}{{=d}x(x+{=p})}$
Cancel the common factors $(x+{=p})$, $(x+{=q})$, $(x-{=q})$ and $x$: $=\frac{1}{{=c}}\times\frac{{=n}}{{=d}}$
Multiply and simplify: $=\frac{{=n}}{{=c*d}}={=r}$
families.notes: Parametrises the book's most repeated exercise (ex1-10-2a/b/c, ex1-11-31f/j; ex1-11-31e has the same skeleton). Skeleton: (x+p)(x+q) / [c(x-q)(x+q)] divided by d*x(x+p) / [n*x(x-q)], with n = r*c*d so the result n/(c*d) = r is a whole number by construction, exactly as in the book (answers 5, 3, 4, 2, 5, 5). The trinomial is written in expanded form x^2+(p+q)x+pq and the student must factorise it; p != q so the trinomial is not a perfect square. Ranges chosen to match the book's magnitudes: q 2..11, p 2..12, largest coefficient n*q <= 100*11 = 1100, as in ex1-11-31j (100d^2-1100d). Verified by exact rational evaluation at several x over all 4800 parameter combinations (answer r, never depends on x). The variable letter is fixed at x (the book varies it; the answer is a number so nothing is lost).

solution: Change the division to multiplication by the reciprocal, that is, flip the second fraction: $\frac{{=a*a}-x^2}{x^2-{=a-b}x-{=a*b}}\times\frac{{=c}x+{=c*b}}{x+{=a}}$
Factorise every numerator and denominator: ${=a*a}-x^2=({=a}-x)({=a}+x)$, $x^2-{=a-b}x-{=a*b}=(x-{=a})(x+{=b})$ and ${=c}x+{=c*b}={=c}(x+{=b})$
Write the product with every factor showing: $\frac{({=a}-x)({=a}+x)}{(x-{=a})(x+{=b})}\times\frac{{=c}(x+{=b})}{x+{=a}}$
Cancel the common factors $({=a}+x)$ and $(x+{=b})$: $=\frac{{=c}({=a}-x)}{x-{=a}}$
Notice that ${=a}-x=-(x-{=a})$, so the two remaining factors cancel and leave a factor of $-1$: $=\frac{-{=c}(x-{=a})}{x-{=a}}=-{=c}$
families.notes: Takes the twist the book itself uses in ex1-10-2k, a difference of squares written the 'wrong way round' (16 - x^2 = (4-x)(4+x)) so that one cancellation leaves (a-x)/(x-a) = -1, and adds the division and a common-factor step that the book's other exercises use. Skeleton: (a^2-x^2)/[(x-a)(x+b)] divided by (x+a)/[c(x+b)]; the middle coefficient of the trinomial is -(a-b), written out by the template. Constraint a - b >= 2 so the trinomial never prints a bare '1x' (and b != a, so the two cancelled linear factors are distinct); b >= 1. The answer is -c, a whole negative number (-2 to -6), so the answer is not the same in every instance. Verified by exact rational evaluation at several x over all 140 parameter combinations. Worked example for a = 5, b = 2, c = 3: (25-x^2)/(x^2-3x-10) divided by (x+5)/(3x+6) equals -3.

solution: The denominators ${=p}$ and ${=q}$ have no common factor, so the lowest common denominator is ${=p}\times {=q}={=p*q}$.

Write each fraction over ${=p*q}$ by multiplying its numerator and its denominator by the missing factor: the first fraction by ${=q}$ and the second by ${=p}$. $\dfrac{x+{=a}}{{=p}}+\dfrac{x+{=b}}{{=q}}=\dfrac{{=q}(x+{=a})}{{=p*q}}+\dfrac{{=p}(x+{=b})}{{=p*q}}$

Put both numerators over the one common denominator and remove the brackets, multiplying every term inside each bracket. $\dfrac{{=q}(x+{=a})}{{=p*q}}+\dfrac{{=p}(x+{=b})}{{=p*q}}=\dfrac{{=q}(x+{=a})+{=p}(x+{=b})}{{=p*q}}=\dfrac{{=q}x+{=q*a}+{=p}x+{=p*b}}{{=p*q}}$
Collect the like terms in the numerator. $\dfrac{{=q}x+{=q*a}+{=p}x+{=p*b}}{{=p*q}}=\dfrac{{=p+q}x+{=q*a+p*b}}{{=p*q}}$

This cannot be simplified further, because the coefficient ${=p+q}$ of $x$ and the denominator ${=p*q}$ have no common factor. So $\dfrac{x+{=a}}{{=p}}+\dfrac{x+{=b}}{{=q}}=\dfrac{{=p+q}x+{=q*a+p*b}}{{=p*q}}$.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Multiplies only the first term of the numerator by the missing factor
proposed_misconceptions.description: When rewriting a fraction over the lowest common denominator, the student multiplies the denominator and the x-term of the numerator by the missing factor but leaves the constant term as it was, as if the factor were not applied to the whole bracket.

families.notes: Basic = the entry point of the skill: add two fractions whose denominators are different small numbers with no common factor (so the LCD is their product), each numerator a linear x + constant, all signs positive. This is the book's own method from ex1-10-3a / ex1-10-2q (LCD, multiply each numerator through, remove brackets, collect like terms) minus the subtraction sign hazard, which stays with the standard-tier book questions; addition of two fractions over their LCD is also what ex1-10-3d and 3f do. Parameters: p in 2..5, q in 2..7, coprime (15 denominator pairs), a and b in 1..6 and different (30 pairs), so 450 instances. Every instance is clean: p+q >= 5 so the x coefficient is never 1 (no '1x' rendering), and gcd(p+q, p*q) = 1 whenever gcd(p, q) = 1, so the final fraction is always in lowest terms and the last solution step is true for every instance. The four options are always pairwise distinct: the correct numerator has x-coefficient p+q >= 5 and constant q*a+p*b, D1 has coefficient 2 and denominator p+q (never equal to p*q for coprime p, q >= 2), D2 has coefficient 2, D3 has the right coefficient but constant a+b, which differs from q*a+p*b because (q-1)*a+(p-1)*b > 0. Distractors: D1 adds numerators and adds denominators (catalogued mc adds-numerators-and-denominators-separately); D2 writes the common denominator p*q but leaves both numerators unscaled, so the x terms add to 2x (catalogued mc numerator-or-whole-number-not-scaled); D3 scales only the x term of each numerator and not the constant, one new misconception declared here. The catalogued mc sign-changed-on-first-term-only needs a subtraction and is not used on this addition-only basic family. mcq is used because every distractor is a specific diagnosable error, not to avoid typing; if the reviewer prefers a typed answer the correct option converts directly to an expression marker.
